title: Circle
tagline: Theorems on chords, arcs, tangents, cyclic quadrilaterals, and angle properties in a circle.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Mathematics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every numerical result in this chapter was independently recomputed. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: A circle is the locus of points in a plane that are at a fixed distance (the radius) from a given point (the centre). This chapter develops the skill of applying circle theorems to find unknown angles, lengths, and relationships between segments, arcs, and chords. The key theorems covered are: the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference; angles in the same segment are equal; the angle in a semicircle is a right angle; radii to the point of tangency are perpendicular to the tangent; and the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord. Cyclic quadrilaterals and their opposite-angle property are also covered.

learningOutcomes: Define a circle and identify its centre, radius, diameter, chord, tangent, and secant.
Apply the seven key circle theorems to find unknown angles and lengths in circle diagrams.
Use the perpendicular-from-centre-to-chord theorem to relate chord length and distance from the centre.
Apply the tangent-radius perpendicular property to solve problems involving tangents.
Use the cyclic quadrilateral opposite-angle theorem: opposite angles sum to 180°.
Find the centre, radius, and equation of a circle given sufficient information.

blocks.text: A circle is the set of all points in a plane that are at a fixed distance (called the radius) from a given point (called the centre). The distance across the circle through the centre is the diameter, which is twice the radius. A chord is a line segment whose endpoints lie on the circle. A diameter is a special chord that passes through the centre. A secant is a line that cuts the circle at two points. A tangent is a line that touches the circle at exactly one point, called the point of contact.
A labelled diagram of a circle showing centre O, radius OA, diameter AB, chord PQ, tangent at T, and secant line XY.

learn.title: Circle Theorem 1: Angle at the Centre

blocks.text: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre of a circle is twice the angle subtended by the same arc at any point on the remaining part of the circle. In symbols, if ∠AOB is the angle at the centre and ∠ACB is the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc AB, then ∠AOB = 2 × ∠ACB.

items.text: In the diagram, O is the centre of the circle, and ∠AOB = 80°. Find ∠ACB, where C is a point on the circle on the larger arc AB.
items.note: By the angle-at-the-centre theorem, the angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre.
By the angle-at-the-centre theorem, the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.

items: The theorem applies to any arc of the circle, not just a semicircle.
The angle at the centre is always twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc.
Be careful to use the correct angle: the angle at the circumference must stand on the same arc as the angle at the centre.
If the angle at the circumference is acute, the angle at the centre is obtuse, and vice versa.

learn.title: Circle Theorem 2: Angles in the Same Segment

blocks.text: Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal. If two angles are subtended by the same chord and stand in the same segment (i.e., their vertices are on the same side of the chord and on the circle), then they are equal.

items.text: In the diagram, chord AB subtends ∠ACB and ∠ADB, where C and D are on the same arc. If ∠ACB = 50°, then ∠ADB = 50°.
items.note: By the angles-in-the-same-segment theorem, angles standing on the same chord and in the same segment are equal.

items.text: In the diagram, ∠AXY = 65° where X and Y are on the circle. Find ∠AZW, where Z and W are on the same segment.
items.note: Both angles stand on the same chord and are in the same segment, so they are equal.

items: The chord must be the same for both angles.
The vertices must be on the same segment (same side of the chord).
If the vertices are on opposite segments, the angles are supplementary (sum to 180°).
This theorem is often used in conjunction with the angle-at-the-centre theorem.

learn.title: Circle Theorem 3: Angle in a Semicircle

blocks.text: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle (90°). If a triangle is inscribed in a circle with one side as the diameter, then the angle opposite that diameter is 90°. In symbols, if AB is a diameter and C is any point on the circle, then ∠ACB = 90°.

items.text: In the diagram, AB is a diameter of the circle, and C is a point on the circle. If ∠ACB = 90°, find the value of x in the diagram where ∠BAC = 35°.
items.note: The angle in a semicircle is 90°. The other two angles of triangle ABC must sum to 90°, so ∠ABC = 90° – 35° = 55°.

items.text: In the diagram, O is the centre of the circle, and AB is a diameter. If ∠ACB = 90°, find ∠OAC given that ∠OCB = 25°.
items.note: Since ∠ACB = 90° and ∠OCB = 25°, we have ∠OCA = 90° – 25° = 65°. Because OA = OC (radii), triangle OAC is isosceles with ∠OAC = ∠OCA = 65°.

items: The side opposite the right angle must be the diameter.
The vertex must lie on the circle (not inside or outside).
This theorem is a special case of the angle-at-the-centre theorem, where the central angle is 180°.
It is frequently used to prove that a triangle is right-angled, or to find an unknown angle in a right triangle inscribed in a circle.

blocks.text: The radius drawn to the point of contact of a tangent is perpendicular to the tangent. If a line touches the circle at T and OT is the radius to the point of contact, then OT ⟂ tangent at T.

items.text: In the diagram, O is the centre, PT is a tangent at T, and OT is the radius. If OT = 5 cm and OP = 13 cm, find the length of PT.
items.note: Since OT ⟂ tangent at T, triangle OTP is right-angled at T. By Pythagoras, OP² = OT² + PT², so PT² = OP² – OT² = 169 – 25 = 144, and PT = 12 cm.

items.text: In the diagram, O is the centre, AB is a chord, and AT is a tangent at A. If ∠AOB = 80°, find ∠BAT.
items.note: Since OA is a radius and AT a tangent, ∠OAT = 90°. In triangle OAB, OA = OB (radii), so ∠OAB = ∠OBA = (180° – 80°) / 2 = 50°. Hence ∠BAT = ∠OAT – ∠OAB = 90° – 50° = 40°. Check: the angle between a tangent and a chord equals half the angle the chord subtends at the centre, 80° / 2 = 40°.

items: The radius to the point of contact is always perpendicular to the tangent.
This theorem is the basis for many problems involving tangents and right triangles.
Pythagoras' theorem is frequently used with this theorem to find unknown lengths.
The angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact equals the angle in the alternate segment (this is a separate but related theorem).

learn.title: Circle Theorem 5: Perpendicular from Centre to Chord

blocks.text: The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord. Conversely, the line joining the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord.

items.text: In the diagram, O is the centre of the circle, AB is a chord, and OM ⟂ AB at M. If OA = 10 cm (radius) and OM = 6 cm, find the length of AB.
items.note: Triangle OAM is right-angled at M. By Pythagoras, OA² = OM² + AM², so AM² = OA² – OM² = 100 – 36 = 64, and AM = 8 cm. Since OM ⟂ AB bisects AB, MB = AM = 8 cm, and AB = 16 cm.

items.text: In the diagram, O is the centre, and two chords AB and CD are equidistant from the centre (i.e., OM = ON where OM ⟂ AB and ON ⟂ CD). If AB = 12 cm, find the length of CD.
items.note: Equal chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre, and conversely, chords equidistant from the centre are equal. Since AB and CD are equidistant from the centre, they have the same length, so CD = 12 cm.

items: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord always bisects the chord.
The converse is also true: the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord.
Equal chords are equidistant from the centre, and chords equidistant from the centre are equal.
Pythagoras' theorem is the primary tool for calculations involving this theorem.

blocks.text: A cyclic quadrilateral is a quadrilateral whose vertices all lie on a circle. The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°. In symbols, if ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, then ∠A + ∠C = 180° and ∠B + ∠D = 180°.

items.text: In the diagram, ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with ∠A = 75° and ∠C = 105°. Verify that opposite angles sum to 180°.
items.note: By the cyclic quadrilateral theorem, opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral always sum to 180°.

items.text: In the diagram, ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. If ∠A = 85° and ∠B = 95°, find ∠D.
items.note: Opposite angles sum to 180°, so ∠A + ∠C = 180° gives ∠C = 180° – 85° = 95°. Then ∠B + ∠D = 180° gives 95° + ∠D = 180°, so ∠D = 85°.

items: All four vertices must lie on the same circle.
Only opposite angles have the supplementary property; adjacent angles do not necessarily sum to 180°.
This theorem is frequently used together with other circle theorems to find unknown angles.
The converse is also true: if opposite angles of a quadrilateral sum to 180°, the quadrilateral is cyclic.

blocks.text: From an external point, exactly two tangents can be drawn to a circle. The two tangents are equal in length. If P is an external point and PT and PS are the two tangents to the circle at T and S respectively, then PT = PS. Also, the line joining the external point to the centre bisects the angle between the two tangents and the angle subtended by the line segment joining the points of contact at the centre.

items.text: In the diagram, P is an external point, and PT and PS are tangents to the circle at T and S. If OT = 6 cm and OP = 10 cm, find the length of PT.
items.note: Radius OT ⟂ tangent PT, so triangle OTP is right-angled at T. By Pythagoras, OP² = OT² + PT², so PT² = OP² – OT² = 100 – 36 = 64, and PT = 8 cm.

items.text: In the diagram, P is an external point, and PT and PS are tangents to the circle. If ∠TPS = 50°, find ∠TOS, where O is the centre.
items.note: In quadrilateral OTPS, ∠OTP = ∠OSP = 90° (radii to tangents), and ∠TPS = 50°. The sum of angles in a quadrilateral is 360°, so ∠TOS = 360° – 90° – 90° – 50° = 130°.

items: From an external point, exactly two tangents can be drawn to a circle.
The two tangents have equal length.
The line from the centre to the external point bisects the angle between the tangents.
The line from the centre to the external point bisects the angle subtended by the chord of contact at the centre.
Pythagoras' theorem is used to find tangent length when the radius and distance from centre are known.

blocks.text: The questions that follow move from basic circle terminology through applying the seven circle theorems to computing unknown angles and lengths to solving problems involving cyclic quadrilaterals and tangents. Work each one by recognising which theorem applies, then state the theorem and the calculation.

questions.prompt: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre of a circle is _____ the angle subtended by the same arc at any point on the remaining part of the circle.
questions.explanation: By the angle-at-the-centre theorem, the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing with the angles-in-the-same-segment theorem, which says those angles are equal.

questions.prompt: The angle in a semicircle is _____.
questions.explanation: The angle in a semicircle is always 90° (a right angle). This is a special case of the angle-at-the-centre theorem where the central angle is 180°.

questions.prompt: If two chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre, then the chords are _____.
questions.explanation: Equal chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre, and conversely, chords equidistant from the centre are equal.

questions.prompt: In the diagram, O is the centre of the circle, AB is a chord, and OM ⟂ AB at M. If OA = 13 cm and OM = 5 cm, find the length of AB.
questions.explanation: Since OM ⟂ AB bisects AB, AM = MB. By Pythagoras in triangle OAM: AM² = OA² – OM² = 13² – 5² = 169 – 25 = 144, so AM = 12 cm. Hence AB = 2 × AM = 24 cm.

questions.prompt: In the diagram, ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with ∠A = 80°. Find ∠C.
questions.explanation: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°, so ∠A + ∠C = 180°, giving ∠C = 180° – 80° = 100°.

questions.prompt: PT is a tangent at T to a circle with centre O. If OT = 4 cm and OP = 5 cm, find PT.
questions.explanation: Radius OT ⟂ tangent PT, so triangle OTP is right-angled at T. By Pythagoras, OP² = OT² + PT², so PT² = OP² – OT² = 25 – 16 = 9, and PT = 3 cm.

questions.prompt: In the diagram, O is the centre of the circle, and AB is a diameter. If ∠BAC = 30°, find ∠ABC.
questions.explanation: AB is a diameter, so the angle it subtends at C is a right angle: ∠ACB = 90°. The angles of triangle ABC add to 180°, so ∠ABC = 180° – 90° – 30° = 60°.

questions.prompt: In the diagram, ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with AB ∥ DC. If ∠B = 70°, find ∠D. Give a reason for your answer.
questions.answer: ∠D = 110°. Reason: In a cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles sum to 180°. Since AB ∥ DC, interior angles on the same side of transversal BC are supplementary, so ∠B + ∠C = 180°. Combining, ∠D = ∠C = 110°.
questions.explanation: Given: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, so ∠B + ∠D = 180° (opposite angles property). Also, AB ∥ DC, so interior angles on the same side of transversal BC satisfy ∠B + ∠C = 180°. From these, ∠C = ∠D = 110°. The first equality uses the cyclic quadrilateral theorem; the parallel-lines property gives the same result.

questions.prompt: Two circles of radii 5 cm and 3 cm touch each other externally. The distance between their centres is:
questions.explanation: When two circles touch externally, their centres and the point of contact lie on one straight line, so the distance between the centres is the sum of the radii: 5 cm + 3 cm = 8 cm.

questions.prompt: A tangent to a circle at point T is perpendicular to the:
options: chord joining T to any point
questions.explanation: The tangent-radius theorem states that the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.

questions.prompt: If two chords of a circle are equal, then their distances from the centre are:
questions.explanation: Equal chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre, and conversely chords equidistant from the centre are equal.

questions.prompt: Angles in the same segment of a circle are:
questions.explanation: Angles subtended by the same chord (or arc) at points on the same segment of the circle are equal.

questions.prompt: The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are:
questions.explanation: In a cyclic quadrilateral, the sum of either pair of opposite angles is 180°.

questions.prompt: The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord ______ the chord.
questions.explanation: A perpendicular drawn from the centre to a chord divides the chord into two equal parts.

questions.prompt: Tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal in ______.
questions.explanation: The lengths of the two tangent segments from an external point to their points of contact with the circle are equal.

questions.prompt: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is ______ the angle subtended by it at any point on the remaining part of the circle.
questions.explanation: By the angle-at-centre theorem, the central angle is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc.

questions.prompt: Two chords AB and CD of a circle intersect at P inside the circle. If ∠APC = 80° and arc AC subtends 50° at the centre, find the angle subtended by arc BD at the centre. Give reasons.
questions.explanation: Angle subtended by arc AC at the circumference is 50°/2 = 25°. In intersecting-chords configuration, ∠APC equals half the sum of angles subtended by arcs AC and BD at the centre? Using the theorem: angle between two chords = 1/2(sum of angles subtended by opposite arcs at centre). So 80° = 1/2(50° + x), giving 160° = 50° + x and x = 110°. Hence arc BD subtends 110° at the centre.

questions.prompt: From an external point P, two tangents PA and PB are drawn to a circle with centre O. If ∠APB = 60°, find ∠AOB and justify your steps.
questions.explanation: OA ⟂ PA and OB ⟂ PB (radius perpendicular to tangent). In quadrilateral OAPB, sum of angles is 360°, so ∠AOB + 90° + 60° + 90° = 360°, giving ∠AOB = 120°. Alternatively, OP bisects ∠APB and ∠AOB in this configuration.

questions.prompt: A student claims that any parallelogram inscribed in a circle must be a rectangle. Analyse this claim and justify whether it is true, stating the theorem used.
questions.answer: The claim is true. In a cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles are supplementary. In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal. Therefore each pair of opposite angles is both equal and supplementary, so each angle is 90°. A parallelogram with all right angles is a rectangle.
questions.explanation: Combining properties of cyclic quadrilaterals (∠A + ∠C = 180°) and parallelograms (∠A = ∠C) forces ∠A = ∠C = 90°, and similarly for the other pair.

questions.prompt: In a circle, chord AB is longer than chord CD. A student concludes that AB is closer to the centre than CD. Analyse the reasoning and state the correct relationship with justification.
questions.answer: The conclusion is correct. The perpendicular distance d of a chord of length l from the centre of a circle of radius r satisfies d² = r² − (l/2)². A longer chord has larger l/2, so smaller d² and hence smaller distance from the centre. Therefore the longer chord AB is nearer to the centre than CD.
questions.explanation: Using Pythagoras in the right triangle formed by radius, half-chord and perpendicular distance shows distance decreases as chord length increases for the same circle.

questions.prompt: Points A, B, C, D lie on a circle in order and ∠ABC + ∠ADC = 190°. Analyse whether ABCD can be a cyclic quadrilateral and explain the result.
questions.answer: ABCD cannot satisfy the cyclic quadrilateral angle property as stated, because for a cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles must sum to exactly 180°. A sum of 190° contradicts this theorem, so either the given measures are inconsistent or the points as described cannot all lie on the same circle with that angle sum.
questions.explanation: The converse and theorem for cyclic quadrilaterals require ∠ABC + ∠ADC = 180°; any other sum indicates the points are not concyclic (given the configuration).

questions.prompt: A tangent is drawn at point A of a circle and a chord AB is drawn. A student measures the angle between the tangent and chord AB and finds it equals the angle in the alternate segment. Analyse why this equality holds.
questions.answer: This is the alternate segment theorem: the angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact equals the angle subtended by the chord in the alternate segment. It follows from the tangent-radius perpendicularity and the angle-at-centre/angle-at-circumference relationship, which together show both angles are equal (each related to half the measure of the intercepted arc).
questions.explanation: Let the tangent at A make angle θ with chord AB; then the central/inscribed angle relations give the angle in the alternate segment as θ, establishing the theorem used in many circle problems.

keyPoints: Equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre and are equidistant from the centre.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord, and conversely the line joining the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to it.
There is one and only one circle passing through three non-collinear points.
The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle subtended by it at any point on the remaining part of the circle.
Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal.
The angle in a semicircle is a right angle.
If a line segment joining two points subtends equal angles at two other points on the same side of the line, the four points are concyclic.
The sum of either pair of opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral is 180°; conversely, if opposite angles are supplementary the quadrilateral is cyclic.
A tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
Tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal in length and make equal angles with the line joining the point to the centre.
examFocus: State the theorem or property used in each step, especially angle-at-centre, angles in the same segment, cyclic quadrilateral and tangent-radius results.
Mark given equal chords, radii, perpendiculars and right angles clearly on the figure before calculating.
Use the fact that all radii of a circle are equal to form isosceles triangles and find base angles.
For tangent problems, draw the radius to the point of contact and apply the right angle with Pythagoras where lengths are involved.
Check whether a quadrilateral is cyclic before using opposite-angle properties; give a reason when concluding concyclicity.
Distinguish between angle at the centre and angle at the circumference on the same arc to avoid doubling errors.
In chord-distance problems, apply the perpendicular from centre bisects chord and then use Pythagoras in the right triangle formed.
Present reasons briefly but precisely (e.g. 'angle in a semicircle', 'tangent ⟂ radius') as required in geometry answers.

vocabulary.meaning: A line segment joining any two points on a circle.
A continuous part of the circumference of a circle.
The region between a chord and the arc it cuts off.
The region bounded by two radii and the arc between them.
A quadrilateral whose all four vertices lie on a circle.
A line that touches a circle at exactly one point.
The point where a tangent touches the circle.
A line that intersects a circle at two distinct points.
Points that lie on the same circle.
An angle formed at a point by lines drawn from the ends of an arc or chord.
The shortest distance from the centre to a chord, measured along a perpendicular.
Half of a circle formed by a diameter and its arc.
